href="https://www.wbez.org/museums/2025/02/12/chicago-history-museum-unionize-employees-union-afscme" target="_blank" ><u>February 2025</u></a>, workers at the museum announced their plans to unionize, joining a wave of organizing at the city’s major cultural institutions. After officially voting to form the union in April of that year, four employees were fired, while others were disciplined or threatened with termination, according to the National Labor Relations Board. This May, the board found the museum <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/work/2026/05/18/chicago-history-museum-labor-law-firing-employees-unionizing-nlrb" target="_blank" ><u>violated federal labor laws</u></a>.</p><p>In an interview Thursday, Anderson said the museum has settled those charges and has extended offers to four employees to return to work. So far, two have accepted the offer, Anderson said.</p><p>Anderson also said the museum has “continued to negotiate in good faith with the union” to reach a collective bargaining agreement, saying “we’ve made a lot of progress since January.”</p><p>A spokesperson with the workers’ union, American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Council 31, confirmed that they had seen “significant progress in the right direction in recent months,” adding that they hope to be able to reach a collective bargaining agreement in the next couple of months.</p><p>The museum has also restored the hours of the four staff members in the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagohistory.org/visit-us/research-center/" target="_blank" ><u>Abakanowicz Research Center</u></a>. Last July, those workers were reduced from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/01/30/chicago-history-museum-ceo-abakanowicz-research-center-city-architecture" target="_blank" ><u>full-time to part-time</u></a>. Now, Anderson said the staff is back to full-time employment.</p><p>The research center has also expanded the hours it is open to the public without appointment. The current summertime hours are noon to 4 p.m. Tuesdays-Fridays. That’s an increase <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/01/30/chicago-history-museum-ceo-abakanowicz-research-center-city-architecture" target="_blank" ><u>from the hours in January</u></a>, which were noon to 3 p.m. Wednesdays-Fridays, by appointment only. Anderson said the center will also be open on Saturdays during the school year.</p><p>“To me, it is one of the most important aspects of the museum, and we need to have it open and available to the public,” Anderson said of the research center.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8b0000" Chicago History Museum is no exception.</p><p>“It is not an easy time for museums and nonprofits, in general. Expenses have drastically increased over the last year,” Anderson said. “We continue to see improvements in attendance and fundraising, but federal funding is still dried up, and so we have some financial headwinds.”</p><p>The federal Institute of Museum and Library Services — which awarded the museum <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/04/09/institute-museum-library-services-funding-kwame-raoul-trump-illinois-library-association-illinois-association-museums-park" target="_blank" ><u>more than $690,000 in grants in fiscal year 2024</u></a> for exhibition and conservation costs — has been under attack by the Trump administration. And last week, the president escalated his <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/24/arts/design/smithsonian-signs-trump-executive-order.html" target="_blank" ><u>attacks against the Smithsonian</u></a>, ordering that signs be installed outside the National Museum of American History “warning visitors about the ideological capture” and correcting the “inaccurate information presented in the museum.”</p><p>Plus, museum leaders nationwide are grappling with advancements in artificial intelligence and what it will mean for the future of their industry. All of this is on Anderson’s mind as he thinks about what comes next for the museum.</p><p>“We want to be thoughtful, fearless and unexpected,” Anderson said. “Sometimes museums, and certainly history museums, are thought to be kind of boring or very scholarly or academic, and I want to embrace new technologies, really deepen community partnerships and present [history] in a kind of a dynamic, playful [way].”</p><p>The museum, which was established in 1856, claims to be the city’s oldest cultural institution. Its collection includes more than 23 million artifacts, documents and images. According to the museum’s board, Anderson was selected from a nationwide pool of more than 70 applicants.</p><p>“Michael is the right person to lead the Museum as cultural institutions nationwide rethink how to offer the best experience possible to visitors and members,” board chair Warren Chapman said in a statement. “People changed their leisure-time habits during the COVID pandemic, and we need to make sure our museum offerings are compelling and meaningful. Michael has the vision and experience to lead these efforts.”</p><p>The Chicago History Museum sees about 150,000 annual visitors. This fall, the museum will launch the exhibition “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagohistory.org/exhibition/threads-of-a-nation-preserving-presidential-clothing/" target="_blank" ><u>Threads of a Nation: Preserving Presidential Clothing</u></a>” featuring garments worn by former presidents George Washington, John Adams and Abraham Lincoln. The pieces are part of the museum’s extensive costume collection.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: Bears WR Rome Odunze backtracks on 'new normal' comment, says foot is 'completely fine'
entries.summary: <p>Alarms went off when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> wide receiver Rome Odunze said last month he was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/03/bears-qb-caleb-williams-giant-leap-will-require-one-from-wr-rome-odunze-as-well" >learning to accept a “new normal”</a> after recovering from a stress fracture in his right foot, and he really wishes he hadn’t phrased it that way.</p><p>It raised questions about whether a player the Bears believed would be a game-changer when they drafted him No. 9 overall in 2024 would have to recalibrate his potential, and that already was a concern after two seasons in which Odunze has been good, but not great.</p><p>He tried to revise his comments — “I just set up a fastball for y’all,” he said with a laugh — after practice Thursday, but that doesn’t necessarily invalidate everything he originally said. With training camp underway, his foot feels “amazing” and he was unwilling to scale back any expectations.</p><p>“It’s not even really something that I think about anymore, which I think is the best thing I think you can have after an injury,” Odunze said. “I know ‘new normal’ has a bunch of connotations of chronic and severe [injury] like it’s never going to be the same, [but] it’s not like that at all. I’m completely fine.”</p><p>He was fast and dynamic Thursday morning with several catches, including an intermediate pass on the left sideline in which he beat cornerback Tyrique Stevenson in zone coverage.</p><p>With injuries like this, though, it always comes down to longevity. Will Odunze hold up once the Bears go to padded practices next week and throughout the grind of the regular season? Nothing he says now will quiet those questions. He has to answer them on the field.</p><p>While he might wish he’d used different terminology, Odunze’s initial “new normal” comments were extensive and detailed. It wasn’t as minor as a mere misspeak.</p><p>He talked about how he’d “never really had an injury like that” and how much it prevented him from running the way he wanted. He said the break created “a different type of foot structure with those bones” going forward. And while he insisted even then that it wouldn’t affect his career trajectory, his expectation was that, “It’s never really back to normal.”</p>

entries.title: Gobernador de Illinois convierte en ley la prohibición de teléfonos celulares en las escuelas
entries.summary: <p>El gobernador JB Pritzker firmó el martes una ley destinada a mantener la mirada de los estudiantes lejos de sus teléfonos y centrada en sus tareas escolares, sumando a Illinois a la lista de estados que prohíben dispositivos que distraen en el salón de clases.</p><p>Todos los distritos escolares locales estarán obligados a instituir prohibiciones de celulares durante toda la jornada escolar, aunque las escuelas secundarias tendrán la opción de limitar el acceso durante el almuerzo y los períodos de cambio de clase, con el fin de restringir “la distracción que los teléfonos inteligentes generan a lo largo del día escolar”, dijo Pritzker en una conferencia de prensa en Elgin.</p><p>“Estamos haciendo que nuestros salones de clase sean más enfocados, más productivos, más propicios para el aprendizaje”, dijo Pritzker, señalando distritos en todo el estado que han implementado sus propias prohibiciones y ya “han visto mejoras en el rendimiento académico, en la participación estudiantil y en el bienestar en general.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6f0000" name="module-6f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“El acoso escolar disminuye, los promedios de calificaciones mejoran, las calificaciones de AP (colocación avanzada) aumentan”, dijo Pritzker antes de firmar una de sus principales prioridades legislativas del año. “Los estudiantes pasan más tiempo conectándose entre sí que esquivándose”.</p><p>La legislación se aprobó fácilmente en la Asamblea General de Illinois durante la sesión de primavera, un año después de haberse estancado en Springfield, mientras que al menos otros 35 estados han restringido el acceso a los celulares en las escuelas.</p><p>La ley de Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/06/02/what-you-need-to-know-about-illinois-new-cellphone-ban-in-schools" target="_blank" >establece excepciones</a> para estudiantes con dispositivos considerados necesarios por profesionales médicos; estudiantes con planes 504 o planes de educación individualizados; estudiantes que aprenden inglés y que los necesitan para la traducción, y clases.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>State of Illinois livestream</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Los maestros también podrán permitir el uso de dispositivos durante las clases y en caso de emergencia. Los distritos deben contemplar el acceso en sus “planos, protocolos o procedimientos de respuesta ante emergencias y crisis”, según la ley.</p><p>Más adelante este verano, la Junta Estatal de Educación de Illinois (ISBE) publicará un modelo de política sobre celulares para fomentar las conversaciones comunitarias en los distritos escolares locales.</p><p>Las escuelas deberán implementar sus propias prohibiciones de celulares al inicio del año académico 2027-28, las cuales se extenderán a tabletas, computadoras portátiles personales, consolas de videojuegos, relojes inteligentes, gafas inteligentes y otros dispositivos electrónicos.</p><p>Los distritos escolares que ya habían impuesto prohibiciones deberán ajustarse plenamente a los estándares estatales para el año escolar 2031-32.</p><p>Casi tres cuartas partes de los profesores de secundaria que respondieron a una encuesta de Pew Research de 2024 calificaron la distracción por teléfonos como un problema mayor.</p><p>La investigación académica preliminar sobre las prohibiciones de celulares ha arrojado resultados mixtos. Un estudio de principios de este año de la <a class="Link" href="https://tom-dee.github.io/files/w35132.pdf" target="_blank" >Oficina Nacional de Investigación Económica (NBER)</a> reveló que una reducción del uso del teléfono tuvo un impacto mínimo en las calificaciones y la asistencia.</p><p>Pero la superintendente Suzanne Johnson, del Distrito Escolar U-46 de Elgin, dijo que el impacto fue evidente cuando su distrito endureció las normas sobre los celulares el año pasado.</p><p>“Al principio nuestros estudiantes probablemente estaban reacios y tal vez no tan contentos, pero se adaptaron rápidamente al nuevo ambiente de aprendizaje”, comentó Johnson en la conferencia de prensa de Pritzker.</p><p>“Sin la distracción de los celulares, los estudiantes se mostraron más participativos, fortalecieron conexiones entre sí y, una vez más, las risas y las conversaciones llenaron nuestros pasillos, nuestra cafetería y nuestros salones. Los maestros nos dijeron que finalmente sintieron que habían recuperado a sus estudiantes”.</p><p>El gobernador coincidió en que la evidencia anecdótica es abundante.</p><p>“Los padres han estado preocupados y han visto ciberacoso y, por supuesto, el impacto en la salud mental que las redes sociales y el uso del teléfono están teniendo en nuestros hijos”, agregó Pritzker. “Los estudiantes comparten esa preocupación”.</p><p>“Queremos asegurarnos de que cada hora de tiempo escolar tenga el mayor impacto positivo posible. Estamos permitiendo que cada niño aprenda plenamente, participe, haga preguntas y desarrolle las habilidades y las relaciones interpersonales que necesita para prosperar”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Westchester man died from heat stress, autopsy finds
entries.summary:
A suburban Westchester man is the latest person whose death has been attributed to heat-related causes this month, according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office.

Robert Feldon, 77, died of heat stress along with complications of a fall, an autopsy determined. He died July 10 at MacNeal Hospital, according to the medical examiner’s office.

At least nine people in Cook County have died from heat-related causes in July, the highest number of deaths in a single year and month in more than a decade, according to a WBEZ and Sun-Times analysis of data from the medical examiner’s office.

The others whose deaths in July have been attributed to the heat are Stephanie Rodriguez, 45; David Gonzalez, 44; Barbara Whigham, 71; Mike Rodriguez, 57; Daniel Machnikowski, 69; Victor Ferguson, 48; David P. Sopys, 46; and Joseph W. Huff, 65.

entries.title: Family mourns Des Plaines woman killed in Fox River boat crash over the weekend
entries.summary: <p>Whenever the weather was clear, Magdalena Jablonska loved heading out on the boat with her fiancé and spending as much time as possible on the water, according to her family.</p><p>But one of those outings turned deadly when Jablonska, of Des Plaines, was killed Saturday after a speeding boat slammed into hers while in a "no wake zone" of the Fox River.</p><p>Now, her family is grieving and trying to come to terms with losing a loved one in a crash caused by another boater.</p><p>“I’m still in disbelief,” said her younger brother Marcin Jablonski. “I just keep thinking that I should have spent more time with her.”</p><p>Jablonski, who lives in North Carolina, said he had gotten a text from his sister just hours before the crash. She had sent him a funny video, something they often did. Jablonki said he never thought he would be getting a call later that day that his sister had died.</p><p>Jablonska, 48, her fiancé, Allen, and their dog, were out on the Fox River in McHenry when they were hit by 45-year-old Richard Stevenson, of Lisle, who was driving his pontoon at an “extremely high rate of speed” around 2:30 p.m., according to the McHenry County State’s Attorney’s Coroner's office. </p><p>Jablonska's fiancé was also injured and was taken to a nearby hospital. He’s has been released and is at home recovering.</p><p>Jablonski said the loss of his sister has been devastating for everyone who loved her. He said his sister was a positive person who always saw the best in others.</p><p>“Whenever she was around you, she just made you feel special,” said Jablonski. “She never had any enemies. Everybody was her friend.”</p><p>Jablonska was born in Poland and moved to the United States in elementary school. After graduating from high school, she joined the U.S. Marine Corps and was stationed in Okinawa.</p><p>Joining the marines was his sister’s way of “challenging herself,” said Jablonski.</p><p>“She to slow down, and we were running. That's when he hit the little boat," Shoevlin said. </p><p>Shoevlin said she immediately called 911 while her husband and son rushed to help pull Jablonska’s fiancé and dog from the water. Her husband tied the small boat to their dock as they waited for police and an ambulance to arrive.</p><p>Afterward, Shoevlin said they grabbed towels from their home to help dry Jablonska’s fiancé and cover her body. The dog was not injured, according to Shoevlin. </p><p>"It's been hard," she said. "My husband is a veteran, and he's seen some stuff, but this one's close to home."</p><p>Stevenson was found in the trees off the shoreline near where his pontoon had come to rest and was placed in custody, said prosecutors. He was charged with one count of reckless homicide and two counts of aggravated DUI causing death.</p><p>Prosecutors said Stevenson’s blood alcohol level was nearly three times the legal limit at the time of the crash.</p><p>Shoevlin said Stevenson was known in the area for his reckless driving. </figure> </div> </div><p>McHenry County Judge Cynthia D. Lamb ordered Stevenson held at a hearing Monday. </p><p>“This man was a ticking time-bomb and that bomb went off this past Saturday on the Fox River," said Deputy Chief Brian Miller during the detention hearing.</p><p>He was expected to appear in court Aug. 5.</p><p>Court records show Stevenson had a history of driving under the influence. He had previously been charged on three occasions with DUI, reckless driving and speeding.</p><p>Stevenson’s attorney could not be reached for comment.</p><p>Jablonski questioned why Stevenson was still allowed to operate any sort of vehicle with his history.</p><p>“How many times does somebody need to repeat the same offense until they’re stopped?” Jablonski asked.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/in-memory-of-magdalena-support-for-dog-shelters" target="_blank" >GoFundMe</a> has been set up in honor of Magdalena Jablonska’s passion for rescuing dogs, with all proceeds going to an animal shelter.</p><p><i>Contributing: Eric White, Sophie Sherry</i></p>

entries.title: 2 people, dog fatally shot inside Harvey home
entries.summary: <p>Two people and a dog were found fatally shot inside a home in far south suburban Harvey early Thursday, authorities said.</p><p>Harvey police officers were called to the home around 7:30 a.m. near 150th Street and Vine Avenue, Harvey Police Chief Dale Mitchell said in a statement. </p><p>Officers found the two people with gunshot wounds, according to the statement. They were pronounced dead at the scene. Two dogs were also shot. One has died and the other was in critical condition. </p><p>No other detail about incident or victims was shared. </p><p>Harvey police were investigating with support from Illinois State Police, according to the statement.</p>

entries.title: Ciudad de Chicago prohíbe que circulen patinetes eléctricos en zona a lo largo del lago
entries.summary: <p>La Ciudad de Chicago ha prohibido los patinetes eléctricos en una vía transitada del vecindario de Edgewater para reducir el número de personas que circulan por las aceras.</p><p>Ya entraron en vigor las restricciones de ubicación virtual para impedir que los scooters eléctricos de Divvy y Lime, rastreados por GPS, circulen por Sheridan Road y sus aceras de Devon Avenue hacia el sur a Bryn Mawr Avenue, dijo la concejal Leni Manaa-Hoppenworth (48.º) la semana pasada.</p><p>La Ciudad dijo que amplió una zona ya existente de prohibición de scooters en el Lakefront Trail para incluir un tramo de 1 milla de Sheridan Road que conecta el vecindario con Lake Shore Drive.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f10000" name="module-f10000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Cualquier scooter de Lime o Divvy que circule por ese tramo de la vía o por la acera se detendrá automáticamente cuando el GPS detecte su ubicación. Las restricciones de ubicación virtual similares han estado vigentes durante años en los senderos del 606 Trail y el Riverwalk y en el Aeropuerto O'Hare.</p><p>El Departamento de Transporte de Chicago (CDOT) implementó las nuevas restricciones de circulación en coordinación con la oficina de Manaa-Hoppenworth "para abordar las preocupaciones de la comunidad sobre la circulación frecuente por las aceras a lo largo de Sheridan", dijo el departamento en un comunicado escrito compartido con <a class="Link" href="https://wgntv.com/news/traffic/new-geofencing-will-limit-e-bikes-and-scooters-in-edgewater/" target="_blank" >WGN News</a>, que informó primero sobre las restricciones.</p><div entries.title: WNBA deletes social media post showing Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers betting on game
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — A social media post showing stars Paige Bueckers and Angel Reese betting $400 on the outcome of a game between their teams "missed the mark," the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba" >WNBA</a> said Thursday.</p><p>The players won't be punished for the bet, a person with direct knowledge of the matter told The Associated Press. The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation.</p><p>The league posted the initial video from All-Star Weekend, days before Bueckers' Dallas Wings and Reese's Atlanta Dream were set to play Wednesday night. The clip featured Bueckers and Reese placing what appeared to be a personal wager on the game. It was presented with the caption, "We did?" with a laughing emoji followed by, "Paige Bueckers on the bet she made with Angel Reese at All-Star Weekend on tonight's matchup."</p><p>The WNBA moved quickly to delete the message, but not before it was shared on social media.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">LMAOO THEY DELETED <a href="https://t.co/1VnX0tUEh2">https://t.co/1VnX0tUEh2</a> <a href="https://t.co/ZNQAvHLJZD">pic.twitter.com/ZNQAvHLJZD</a></p>— correlation (@nosyone4) <a href="https://x.com/nosyone4/status/2082599409481637967?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>"While the social media post was intended to be lighthearted, WNBA players are well aware of the league's policies prohibiting betting on WNBA games and receive training every year reinforcing those policies," a league spokesperson said Thursday. "We recognized that the post missed the mark, removed it shortly after it was published, and addressed the matter internally.</p><p>"We will also use this as an opportunity to reemphasize with the players involved that conversations about wagering on WNBA games, even when intended as a joke, can have negative consequences."</p><p>The Wings and the Dream both deferred to the league statement when asked for comment.</p><p>The league's collective bargaining agreement states that any kind of wagering is strictly prohibited and that players can be fined, suspended or even disqualified from the WNBA at the sole discretion of the commissioner.</p><p>The Dream rallied from a 15-point deficit to beat the Wings 82-81 on Wednesday, with Reese notching 22 points and 12 rebounds and Bueckers finishing with 16 points and six assists.<br></p>

entries.title: Illinois SNAP recipients kicked off the federal food program are getting $400 from the state
entries.summary: <p>Thousands of people who lost federal food assistance due to expanded work rules will receive a one-time $400 benefit starting Saturday, according to state officials.</p><p>The Families Receiving Emergency Support for Hunger, or FRESH, program will provide support to an estimated 100,000 people in Illinois who were deemed ineligible for the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP, as of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/30/snap-food-assistance-cutoffs-begin-friday-in-illinois-what-you-need-to-know" target="_blank" ><u>May 1</u></a>. The state allocated $70 million for the program in the budget passed this year, with one $400 benefit allowed per household.</p><p>Congress expanded the work rules for the SNAP program to include 55- to 64-year-olds, veterans and parents whose youngest child is age 14 or older. Since those rules went into effect in Illinois, about 148,000 people have lost food assistance, according to the Illinois Department of Human Services, which administers the program and will also distribute FRESH funds.</p><p>Overall, participation in the SNAP program in Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/27/illinois-sees-16-drop-in-snap-enrollment-one-year-after-food-program-overhaul" target="_blank" ><u>declined by 16%</u></a> since last summer when President Donald Trump signed into law the bill that overhauled the program.</p><p>Households eligible for the FRESH program do not have to apply, according to state officials. The funds will be distributed through LINK cards, which is how SNAP recipients receive funds to buy groceries.</p><p>“In Illinois, we passed the FRESH program to help provide some relief for families kicked off food assistance, but no state can backfill the cruel and imminent cuts set in motion by Trump’s budget bill,” Gov. JB Pritzker said in a prepared statement.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/27/illinois-sees-16-drop-in-snap-enrollment-one-year-after-food-program-overhaul" >Illinois sees 16% drop in SNAP enrollment 1 year after food program overhaul</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Elvia Malagón

entries.title: Illinois registra una caída del 16% en la inscripción en SNAP un año después de los cambios al programa
entries.summary: <p>Manos pequeñas ayudaron a cargar cinco cajas de comida en el baúl de la camioneta de Irene Salinas Torres.</p><p>“Yo cargué esta”, dijo orgulloso un niño.</p><p>Salinas Torres y su familia se detuvieron en una organización sin fines de lucro en Pilsen para la distribución mensual de alimentos esta primavera, poco después de que se esperara que miles perdieran el acceso al programa federal de Asistencia Nutricional Suplementaria (SNAP) por la ampliación de las reglas laborales y otras nuevas restricciones aprobadas por el Congreso el verano pasado. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ea0000" name="module-ea0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La madre de cinco hijos había recibido $450 en beneficios de SNAP cada mes hasta aproximadamente marzo.</p><p>“Nos limitamos en muchas cosas”, dijo Salinas Torres. Perdió el programa SNAP porque los ingresos de su hogar aumentaron cuando un hijo mayor empezó a trabajar. “Solo compramos lo esencial, lo que necesitas para comer ese día. No tenemos el lujo de comprar extra”.</p><p>En el último año, el programa SNAP en Illinois ha disminuido un 16%. Para junio, el número de beneficiarios de SNAP había caído a casi 1.6 millones, desde casi 1.9 millones el año pasado, según el Departamento de Servicios Humanos de Illinois (IDHS). Ese es el número más bajo de personas que reciben asistencia alimentaria en el estado desde 2009.</p><p>Quienes permanecen son una población vulnerable. Casi el 97% de las personas que todavía reciben SNAP fueron exentas de las reglas laborales ampliadas porque cumplen ciertos requisitos, como convivir con una condición física o mental o tener un niño de 13 años o menos, según el estado.</p><p>IDHS, que administra el programa a nivel local, estima que 148,000 personas perdieron SNAP debido a los requisitos laborales en los últimos meses. Los funcionarios estatales habían estimado inicialmente que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/01/22/con-nuevas-reglas-de-snap-en-el-horizonte-funcionarios-del-condado-de-cook-advierten-sobre-las-consecuencias" target="_blank" >400,000 personas</a> perderían los beneficios. En el último año, otras 157,000 personas perdieron beneficios además de las 148,000 debido a cambios en el ingreso del hogar, cambios en cuáles <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/10/familias-refugiadas-son-el-grupo-mas-reciente-que-enfrenta-el-recorte-de-los-beneficios-alimentarios-de-snap" target="_blank" >inmigrantes pueden acceder al programa</a> u otras razones.</p><p>A los beneficiarios de SNAP en Illinois les ha ido mejor que en estados que han recortado sus programas. Arizona ha registrado una disminución del 50% en el número de beneficiarios de SNAP.</p><p>Este mes se cumple un año desde que el presidente Donald Trump firmó la ley H.R. 1, un gran plan de impuestos y gasto que impuso estos cambios a SNAP y que también busca transferir de forma drástica los costos del programa a los estados. Desde entonces, la inscripción en SNAP ha caído más rápido a nivel nacional de lo que el gobierno anticipaba, con estados reduciendo los registros mientras se preparan para una mayor carga de costos, dijo Ty Jones Cox, vicepresidente de asistencia alimentaria del Centro de Prioridades Presupuestarias y Políticas, un instituto de políticas públicas con sede en Washington, D.C.</p><p>“SNAP está en medio de la disminución más pronunciada y rápida de la participación en décadas, y no es porque la necesidad sea menor”, dijo Jones Cox, señalando que la inscripción no había caído tan rápido desde 1997, durante reformas previas al programa de asistencia alimentaria.</p><p>En Illinois, la inscripción en SNAP había tendido al alza de forma sostenida desde inicios de los 2000, a medida que un programa de asistencia en dinero en efectivo llamado Asistencia Temporal para Familias Necesitadas (TANF) se redujo drásticamente tras la reforma de la asistencia social de 1996. SNAP se convirtió en uno de los principales programas de red de seguridad de los que dependían muchos hogares de bajos ingresos, dijo James Ziliak, director fundador del Centro de Investigación sobre la Pobreza de la Universidad de Kentucky.</p><p>En Chicago, hay señales crecientes de que la inseguridad alimentaria este año está afectando a los residentes. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/21/save-a-lot-stores-set-to-close-saturday-after-years-of-turmoil-recent-ceo-death-threatens-city-funded-deal" target="_blank" >Las tiendas de comestibles de descuento Save A Lot</a> citaron los recortes a SNAP como una razón para cerrar locales. En el oeste de la ciudad, una despensa registra un aumento de las filas por comida y de los pedidos en línea. Grupos que trabajan con personas con discapacidades físicas y de salud mental están dedicando largas jornadas a ayudar a sus clientes a recuperar sus beneficios de SNAP.</p><p>Para personas como Salinas Torres, la necesidad de comida no ha desaparecido. Era su primera vez en la despensa organizada por el Centro Infantil y Familiar El Hogar del Niño de la organización sin fines de lucro Brightpoint y fue un alivio. Hace poco se había llevado a sí misma al hospital después de sentirse tan estresada por las finanzas de su hogar.</p><p>“Me siento presionada preguntándome si lo vamos a lograr hoy o no”, contó. “Cuando me hablaron de esta despensa, pensé que era una forma de no preocuparme durante al menos una semana”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> </div><p></p><h3>Una red de seguridad que se contrae</h3><p>Hace apenas unos años, durante la pandemia de COVID-19, los beneficios de SNAP se ampliaron —y la idea de cómo debería el gobierno apoyar a los residentes se amplió—, dijo Carolyn Barnes, profesora asociada de la Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy and Practice de la Universidad de Chicago.</p><p>“En los últimos cinco años, la red de seguridad, tal como la conocen las familias de bajos ingresos, ha oscilado”, dijo Barnes. “Pasó de ser súper accesible y generosa de manera sin precedentes, a ser ahora increíblemente difícil de acceder y vulnerable a más recortes”.</p><p>Este patrón —expansión seguida de contracción— ha ocurrido durante décadas, dijo Barnes. Una diferencia ahora es la rapidez con la que se llevaron a cabo las reformas de SNAP, incluidas en la H.R. 1, comparada con los esfuerzos de reforma de la asistencia social en los años 90.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-250000" name="html-embed-module-250000"></a><div style="min-height:537px" id="datawrapper-vis-dVP57"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/dVP57/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-dVP57"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/dVP57/full.png" alt="SNAP enrollment grew over time as welfare rolls shrunk in Illinois (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>“Muchos estados no conocían el impacto potencial de muchos de estos cambios administrativos [de SNAP]”, dijo Barnes. “Así que mucho de esto se siente apresurado y menos como una campaña planificada y concertada de 20 años que llevó a la reforma de la asistencia social”.</p><p>En 1996, el entonces presidente Bill Clinton, un demócrata, firmó cambios a la reforma de la asistencia social que pretendían reducir la dependencia de la ayuda gubernamental y empujar a la gente al mercado laboral, según un análisis de la Brookings Institution, una organización sin fines de lucro de políticas públicas en Washington, D.C.</p><p>Pero muchos interpretaron la reforma como un ataque a las mujeres negras, dijo Barnes.</p><p>“La retórica de la reina del bienestar que [el presidente Ronald] Reagan popularizó”, dijo Barnes, “esto iba sobre autosuficiencia, responsabilidad familiar; los padres deben involucrarse en el cuidado de sus hijos”.</p><p>La reforma apuntó al programa de asistencia social que se convirtió en TANF. Este ofrece asistencia financiera por un periodo limitado a mujeres embarazadas y familias para pagar comida, vivienda y servicios públicos.</p><p>Un año después de esa reforma, la inscripción en TANF en Illinois disminuyó alrededor de un 12%, según datos del Centro de Investigación sobre la Pobreza de la Universidad de Kentucky. A largo plazo, las cifras se desplomaron.</p><p>Las familias con TANF habían sido inscritas automáticamente en SNAP antes de la reforma, pero eso cambió después de 1996. En lugares como Illinois, eso provocó una caída en la inscripción a la asistencia alimentaria, de 1.1 millones de personas en 1995 a 760,472 personas cinco años después, según datos del centro.</p><p>Eso pudo deberse en parte a que las familias en TANF abandonaron ambos programas, agregó Ziliak. En los años siguientes, sólo alrededor de la mitad de los elegibles para la asistencia alimentaria estaban inscritos, dijo, por lo que hubo un impulso para inscribir a la gente. De 2004 a 2024, siempre hubo más de 1 millón de personas recibiendo asistencia alimentaria en Illinois, con picos de 2 millones en 2013 y en 2023.</p><p>Mientras tanto, los números de TANF siguieron desplomándose. Para 2024 —tres décadas después de la reforma de la asistencia social— sólo había 20,022 residentes de Illinois inscritos. La participación desde la era de Clinton disminuyó un 96%.</p><p>“Lo que sí sabemos, según lo que podemos captar en las encuestas, es que sus ingresos familiares totales disminuyeron después de la reforma del bienestar”, dijo Ziliak.</p><h3>Los estados enfrentan una pesada carga financiera</h3><p>En este primer año de la reforma de SNAP, el estado de Illinois ha tratado de mantener a la mayor cantidad posible de personas en el programa de asistencia alimentaria, en contraste con otros estados que han trabajado a la carrera para cumplirlo haciendo más difícil que los hogares sigan siendo elegibles.</p><p>Pero lo que trae la H.R. 1 son nuevos requisitos de compartir costos para los estados, lo que ejercerá una creciente presión financiera sobre Illinois y otros estados.</p><p>Para empezar, los funcionarios de Illinois estiman que una disposición implica unos $80 millones anuales en nuevos costos administrativos.</p><p>También hay una sanción importante en el horizonte. A partir del año fiscal 2029, o en el otoño de 2028, Illinois podría ser responsable de hasta $550 millones anuales en nuevos costos, según un <a class="Link" href="https://civicfed.org/blog/illinois-fails-lower-snap-payment-error-rates-targeted-hr-1" target="_blank" >análisis de la Civic Federation</a>. Illinois, junto con defensores y otros estados sujetos a esta penalidad, presionan para que esos castigos se retrasen hasta 2030.</p><p>La penalidad corresponde a una llamada “tasa de error” de SNAP que se considera alta. Esa tasa se calcula a partir de una pequeña muestra de casos y se utiliza para medir pagos excesivos o insuficientes de beneficios, según IDHS. La medición ha existido por décadas, pero nunca antes se había usado para trasladar costos a los estados. La administración de Trump dice que la usa para impulsar mayor precisión y eficiencia.</p><p>Los estados con una tasa superior al 6% deberán pagar una parte de los beneficios de SNAP. La tasa más reciente de Illinois fue casi del 15%, según el Departamento de Agricultura (USDA). Los funcionarios estatales compartieron esfuerzos para reducir ese porcentaje, incluyendo mejoras tecnológicas y la incorporación de trabajadores de casos, pero en un comunicado descartaron los objetivos declarados por la administración de Trump, calificándolo de "esquema de sanciones" que se está usando para "exprimir miles de millones de dólares de los contribuyentes estatales".</p><p>La presión para reducir la tasa de error parece estar impulsando algunos cambios drásticos en la inscripción en lugares como Arizona, donde los funcionarios están exigiendo más documentación para obtener asistencia alimentaria, según informó <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/20/us/politics/snap-food-stamps-arizona.html?unlocked_article_code=1.zlA.8Wwh.DvlJy4sEAVoD&smid=url-share" target="_blank" >The New York Times</a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e74bcc" West Garfield Park, una fila rodeó la despensa Above and Beyond en mayo, justo después de que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/01/los-recortes-en-la-asistencia-alimentaria-de-snap-ya-comenzaron-en-illinois-y-esto-es-lo-que-necesitas-saber" target="_blank" >comenzaran los recortes de beneficios</a>. Al menos dos personas estaban entre quienes perdieron los beneficios de SNAP. Un hombre dijo que ahora pasa por la despensa tres o cuatro veces a la semana.</p><p>Above and Beyond ha visto un aumento del 11% en el número de personas que buscan comida en comparación con esta época del año pasado, dijo su director ejecutivo Ken Cozzi. Es difícil saber si la demanda se debe exclusivamente a los cambios en SNAP, pero han escuchado a muchas personas hacer lo que pueden para estirar cualquier dinero y fondos que reciben.</p><p>La despensa destaca porque ya está abierta seis días a la semana. Y con las despensas preparándose para una mayor necesidad debido a los cambios en SNAP, declaró Cozzi, es difícil ver cómo podrían expandirse aún más.</p><p>“Están quitando un nivel entero de beneficios para muchas personas donde ahora es estrictamente despensas, nada más intermedio”, agregó Cozzi.</p><p>En el vecindario de West Town, cajas llenas de avena, arroz y atún estaban apiladas en tarimas dentro de la sede de Nourishing Hope. Las cajas formaban parte de pedidos en línea, cuya demanda ha crecido entre un 130% y un 140% desde que se anunciaron los cambios a SNAP el año pasado, dijo Natia Barnett, gerente principal de expansión de programas de la organización sin fines de lucro que también opera despensas.</p><p>Durante los últimos tres años, Nourishing Hope se ha asociado con organizaciones comunitarias para distribuir más alimentos en los vecindarios, dijo Barnett. Las personas hacen pedidos en línea que se recogen en centros comunitarios y la demanda ha crecido allí también. El Hogar del Niño se unió al programa en mayo y planea expandirse.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ken Cozzi es el director ejecutivo de la despensa gratuita Above and Beyond en West Garfield Park. Ya están abiertos seis días a la semana. Dice que le resulta difícil ver cómo pueden hacer más para atender la creciente demanda.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Sigue la necesidad de alimentos y apoyo</h3><p>Las exenciones amplias en Illinois han disminuido el número de personas que el estado anticipaba que perderían asistencia alimentaria este verano, pero los trabajadores sociales locales están viendo a personas que luchan por mantener sus beneficios.</p><p>El personal de Association House of Chicago en Humboldt Park empezó a escuchar a sus clientes en mayo cuando de repente se encontraron sin beneficios.</p><p>Eso “obligó a personas con discapacidades a volver y pelear por algo que deberían haber seguido recibiendo de todos modos”, dijo Maggie Hettman, quien trabaja en la división de salud conductual. “Y mucha de nuestra gente tiene problemas de salud mental. Se puede entender que eso las arrojó a una espiral... Las personas con discapacidades físicas a veces no pueden ir por su cuenta, sentarse en la oficina de DHS durante horas”.</p><p>Y eso ha significado que los gestores de casos deben pasar tiempo acompañando a sus clientes a citas médicas para obtener papeleo que acredite una exención, o bien dedicar días enteros a una oficina de DHS, dijo Mary González, quien trabaja en el equipo de tratamiento y apoyo comunitario. Otros que lograron que les restauraran los beneficios descubrieron que ahora reciben menos que antes, dijeron González y Hettman.</p><p>Otros clientes están atrapados en la paradoja de tratar de cumplir los requisitos laborales mientras esperan obtener la designación de discapacidad para poder ser exentos. Hay alrededor de 60 personas en una lista de espera para recibir ayuda para solicitar la discapacidad ante la Administración del Seguro Social, lo que podría ser un proceso de uno a dos años, dijo Hettman.</p><p>“Es simplemente decepcionante ver a la población que más necesita ayuda sin poder acceder a ella”, dijo González.</p><p>Algunas personas han logrado que les restablezcan los beneficios.</p><p>Salinas Torres, la madre de cinco, volvió a tener SNAP en junio después de que se recalculó el ingreso de su hogar. Ahora recibe $800 al mes en beneficios alimenticios.</p><p>“Me siento mejor”, dijo aliviada Salinas Torres.</p><p>Pero todavía planea usar la distribución mensual en El Hogar del Niño para ayudar a alimentar a su familia.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Art Institute of Chicago workers' union pushes back against museum's pending custodial contract
entries.summary: <p>As thousands of Lollapalooza fans descended on Grant Park on Thursday afternoon, members of the Art Institute of Chicago Workers United handed out bilingual fliers to them that read, “Give AIC custodians their jobs back.”</p><p>Last month, the Art Institute <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/22/art-institute-of-chicago-backlash-outsource-custodial-staff-afscme-union-museum-labor" >decided to outsource the jobs</a> of approximately 23 custodial workers starting Aug. 15, and the museum has faced strong backlash over the move.</p><p>“We're out here to say it's not fair,” said Cameron Day, staff representative of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Council 31, the union’s bargaining unit. “We want to have a conversation. Let's keep these workers in-house here at the Art Institute of Chicago.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a That union has contracts to protect wages, paid time off and benefits.</p><p>At a July 22 all-staff meeting, Art Institute President James Rondeau answered questions from employees about what’s next for the institution after the change.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SJYU62bP4q4" target="_blank" >video</a> of the meeting showed things got heated after Rondeau told staff, "Do you want a promise of job security and a raise today or no? entries.title: Lawyer for man shot by Chicago police officer disputes whether he got into gunfight with cops
entries.summary: <p>A lawyer for a man wounded in what officials have described as a shootout with Chicago police said Thursday that version of events was “absolutely not true."</p><p>Malik Wrightsell, 34, is accused of pulling a gun out of a bag and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/05/chicago-man-charged-with-attempted-murder-after-cpd-involved-shooting" target="_blank" >firing once at two cops</a> after fleeing a traffic stop earlier this month in South Shore.</p><p>One of the officers was struck in their bulletproof vest, Cook County prosecutors have said. The officer then returned fire, hitting Wrightsell multiple times. Prosecutors said the other cop was also shot in his elbow during the exchange of gunfire.</p><p>Wrightsell’s attorney, Cierra Norris, told reporters gathered outside police headquarters that she and her client’s family “believe confidently that after our investigation ... that is going to be revealed as not being what happened.”</p><p>Norris argued that a struggle had ensued after “an illegal foot chase,” and “a firearm went off.”</p><p>Wrightsell was stopped the morning of July 3 while driving a “non-street legal vehicle” in the 2000 block of East 79th Street, according to a statement from the Civilian Office of Police Accountability. Prosecutors later described it as a “dune buggy style vehicle” that lacked proper registration and was not allowed on the street.</p><p>Norris said Wrightsell is “known throughout his community” for creating go-carts and motorbikes. She said he was bringing one of those vehicles to his son’s sixth birthday party when he was stopped.</p><p>A check revealed Wrightsell didn’t have any insurance or registration for the vehicle, according to prosecutors. When officers returned and ordered him out of the vehicle he fled within seconds, prosecutors said.</p><p>According to Norris, Whitesell “was scared, and so he ran.”</p><p>Officers caught up to him in an alley, where the struggle and ensuing shooting incident happened, COPA said.</p><p>Norris wouldn’t address whether Wrightsell had a firearm, but she argued the official narrative is “absolutely not true.”</p><p>“It's our contention that the bullet that harmed a Chicago police officer did not come from Malik,” Norris said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Under city law, the agency has up to 60 days to release the footage.</p><p>“We want the full bodycam,” said Wrighsell’s sister, Ardice Marshall. “We want to see it intact, we want to see exactly what happened. We want the world to see, as they all labeled him a shooter, a police killer, a police officer shooter.</p><p>"Let the bodycam show what we all know about him, that he was in fear for his life … and this just took a turn.”</p><p>Wrightsell has been charged with attempted first-degree murder, aggravated battery to a peace officer, aggravated assault of a peace officer, resisting or obstructing a peace officer and two weapons offenses. He also received a ticket for operating a non-highway vehicle, court records show.</p><p>He was ordered detained pending trial.</p><p>“It's not fair that Malik is being held in Cook County [Jail] on trumped-up charges to cover up Chicago Police Department's own shortcomings and civil-rights violations,” Norris said.</p>

entries.title: Big series vs. Cardinals shows what Cubs can do when Alex Bregman is hot: ‘Hopefully, I keep that rolling’
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> have managed one of baseball’s best records, all while dealing with pitching injuries and a monthlong early-summer slump.</p><p>They’re <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/29/cubs-offense-stats-rankings-bats-lineup-ian-happ-dansby-swanson-jed-hoyer-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-pitching" >one of baseball’s best offensive teams</a>, third in the sport in runs scored coming into Thursday’s 4-2 extra-inning win over the Cardinals, looking capable of achieving their championship-level goals, should <b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >fortify the pitching staff</a> ahead of Monday’s trade deadline.</p><p>They’ve done it all with big-money free-agent addition <b>Alex Bregman</b> hitting nowhere close to how he’d like, nowhere near the kinds of numbers he’s put up in his career.</p><p>But how high can they fly if Bregman turns it on?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">From the Missouri side of the Mighty Mississipp’ it’s a couple two, tree things about the Cubs. <a href="https://x.com/suntimes_sports?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@suntimes_sports</a> <a href="https://t.co/PyPzvg0Aka">pic.twitter.com/PyPzvg0Aka</a></p>— Vinnie Duber (@VinnieDuber) <a href="https://x.com/VinnieDuber/status/2082968412859326845?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Cubs got a glimpse at what a red-hot Bregman bat looks like this week. Their third baseman had a monster series, with 10 hits in 19 trips to the plate across four games. Seven of those hits went for extra bases, including the RBI double that proved Thursday’s game-winner.</p><p>A lack of power has been the main gripe as Bregman has searched for his footing with his new club. Coming into Thursday, his .375 slugging percentage was far and away the lowest of his career.</p><p>But this week’s version was the Bregman the Cubs thought they’d be getting when they shelled out $175 million in the offseason.</p><p>“He’s been a productive part of the offense, even as he hasn’t hit the way he wants to hit,” left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> said Tuesday. “The back of his baseball card shows [what it shows].</p><p>“He’s that type of player. He’s been working really hard on it, it’s good to see him get some results. We’re all pretty confident that at the end of the year, it’s going to look pretty similar to what it looks like every year.”</p><p>Those votes of confidence have been the norm from Bregman’s teammates all season, thanks to the two-time World Series champ’s long track record of major league success.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Alex Bregman gives the Cubs the lead in the 10th 👏 <a href="https://t.co/nF8DUoES03">pic.twitter.com/nF8DUoES03</a></p>— Marquee Sports Network (@WatchMarquee) <a href="https://x.com/WatchMarquee/status/2082935846768869460?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Certainly, it’ll take more than a sizzling four-game stretch for Bregman to count as the potent presence in the lineup that was planned, but this was a tantalizing snapshot.</p><p>“He had a very good offensive series. That’s something to build on, for sure,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “It’s confidence-building, and it’s good for us winning baseball games, as you saw this week.”</p><p>“I felt like it was quality at-bat after quality at-bat,” Bregman said. “Hopefully, I keep that rolling.”</p><h3><b>‘A different guy every day’</b></h3><p>Bregman’s review of the Cubs’ bullpen?</p><p>“It’s been awesome,” he said. “It’s a different guy every day.”</p><p>He doesn’t know how right he is.</p><p>Righty <b>Aaron Civale</b> became the 13th different Cubs pitcher to earn a save Thursday, setting a new club mark for the most in a single season.</p><p>“It’s just our journey this year with our bullpen,” Counsell said. “I give <b>Jacob Webb</b> a lot of credit in this thing, how he’s kind of handled whatever has been put in front of him.</p><p>“For the last three months, it’s been the biggest out in the game. He’s handled those outs. I give Jacob a lot of credit in making it possible.”</p><h3><b>Birthday boy</b></h3><p>Righty pitcher <b>Javier Assad</b> celebrated his 29th birthday with 4⅓ innings of one-run ball Thursday, his latest solid effort.</p><p>He’s bounced back and forth between the bullpen and the rotation this season, proving himself incredibly valuable in helping to keep an injury-ravaged staff afloat.</p><p>“There’s going to be players that have to have this flexibility,” Counsell said. “It’s kind of why I use the ‘out-getter’ word because you have to have people that are able to do both.”</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Sky's biggest trade deadline need isn't a player, it's a way out of the Mystics pick swap
entries.summary: <p>The trade deadline is coming up Aug. 2, a time when teams can add talent for a playoff push, trade away veterans to build for the future or, as is far more common in the WNBA, stand pat.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> coach Tyler Marsh didn't tip his hand on what the team might do, saying he is focused on the players he has. He said he wasn't expecting many moves around the league, citing salary cap constraints and teams "outside of the Sky" being reluctant to part with draft capital.</p><p>When asked what type of player he would add if it came at no cost, he laughed.</p><p>"A'ja Wilson."</p><p>Can't fault him for dreaming about the league's best player. And dreaming might be the Sky's best escape from a past deal that has come back to haunt them.</p><p>The Sky entered the post-All-Star portion of the season in 13th place. Ordinarily, a team in that position could trade productive veterans for draft capital and turn its attention toward the future.</p><p>But because of a pick swap they agreed to with the Mystics in 2024, the Sky do not have that luxury. They need to make the playoffs or risk sending away what could be a top-three pick.</p><p>The Sky currently have the second-best odds at the No. 1 pick in the 2027 draft. The Mystics, meanwhile, hold the final playoff spot, with a 67.8% chance of keeping it, according to ESPN. If those trajectories continue, the Sky would hand over a potential top-three pick and get back a late first-rounder.</p><p>More than any player or pick, what the Sky need at the deadline is a way out of that bind.</p><p>If they could somehow convince Washington to relinquish the swap rights, it would restore flexibility. The Sky could still shoot for a miracle playoff run. But if they fall short, they would at least have a lottery pick to add to their young core.</p><p>So what could entice the Mystics into a deal?</p><p>Washington could use help at point guard, and the Sky have a good one in Skylar Diggins. But Diggins is injured and signed to an expensive two-year contract. Plus, a veteran guard might not be enough to pry away a pick with a legitimate chance of landing franchise-altering young talents such as Juju Watkins (USC), Madison Booker (Texas), or Hannah Hidalgo (Notre Dame).</p><h3><b>How did the Sky get here?</b></h3><p>The Sky traded the 2027 swap, along with the No. 3 pick in the 2025 draft, to Washington for Ariel Atkins. Atkins was supposed to help elevate the Sky into a winning team in 2025, and the swap was supposed to be innocuous because the Mystics appeared a long way off from playoff contention.</p><p>Neither bet panned out.</p><p>The Sky missed the playoffs last season, and the Mystics arrived ahead of schedule. Atkins was later traded to the Sparks for Rickea Jackson.</p><p>General manager Jeff Pagliocca <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/03/amid-losing-season-sky-gm-jeff-pagliocca-still-sees-playoff-potential-and-an-underrated-young-core" >told the Sun-Times on July 3</a> that the swap is "on his mind at all times," but he did not express regret. He said he would make that deal "every single time," because it ultimately brought them Jackson.</p><p>"If that [swap] costs a few spots ultimately — which isn't even guaranteed yet — I feel passionate about where our team is going and what our trajectory is," Pagliocca said.</p><h3><b>Could the Sky make a different deal?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Sky's position makes them unlikely to take a major swing. But they could tweak around the margins, perhaps by finding a trade partner for backup center Elizabeth Williams, who could give a playoff team frontcourt depth, in return for draft capital. </p><p>Or they could use one or both of the first-round picks they acquired from the Dream to add a player.</p><p>More likely, the Sky's best "trade deadline addition" is one they'll make without a deal: the return of injured guard DiJonai Carrington.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Ahead of expected trade-deadline pitching adds, Cubs starters rolling: ‘A lot of talent in our rotation’
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — Presumably, there are new pitchers coming the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ way.</p><p>Jed Hoyer’s front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >will be focusing on adding arms</a> ahead of Monday’s trade deadline, at the very least attempting to infuse depth into a roster that’s stretched it to the limits at times this season.</p><p>If Hoyer & Co. decide to go really big — Tarik Skubal, anyone? — there could be a new name at the top of the Cubs’ rotation.</p><p>But in the days leading up to the deadline, the Cubs are getting really good performances from their existing starting staff.</p><p>Excluding the poor performance of veteran righty Jameson Taillon, who was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/27/cubs-jameson-taillon-dfa-mlb-trade-deadline-pitching-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-rotation" >designated for assignment this week</a>, the Cubs are riding a string of exceptional starting efforts, with top-of-the-rotation lefties Matthew Boyd and Shota Imanaga, in particular, looking like the kinds of arms who could power playoff victories come October.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">From the Missouri side of the Mighty Mississipp’ it’s a couple two, tree things about the Cubs. <a href="https://x.com/suntimes_sports?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@suntimes_sports</a> <a href="https://t.co/PyPzvg0Aka">pic.twitter.com/PyPzvg0Aka</a></p>— Vinnie Duber (@VinnieDuber) <a href="https://x.com/VinnieDuber/status/2082968412859326845?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“We have a lot of talent in our rotation,” Boyd said after throwing seven scoreless innings in Wednesday’s extra-inning loss to the Cardinals. “Guys are continuing to build off of good performances, to grow and adapt from what we do in a positive way.</p><p>“We have a very good rotation with the guys that are in here. If guys are added, that’s always welcome. It’s going to make us better.”</p><p>Boyd has been especially noteworthy for what he’s done since returning from a nearly two-month stay on the injured list while recovering from knee surgery. He’s only made a dozen starts this season, his last seven coming since the end of his IL trip. In those outings, he’s got a spectacular 1.93 ERA, with the Cubs winning all but once.</p><p>Boyd went at least six innings in all five of his starts this month, allowing one run or fewer in four of them.</p><p>The veteran southpaw, an All-Star last season, continues to wince in frustration at the mention of the time he missed, but he sees the silver lining: that he’ll be in good physical shape when the games are the most important.</p><p>“Anytime you’re out there every five days, it’s an awesome opportunity to stay in that rhythm and continue to build off the start before,” he said. “My job is to be out there, and it’s more conducive to do that versus being on the IL.</p><p>“The one side of being on the IL is you save some bullets in those situations. I definitely feel fresh, definitely feel good. That’s a silver lining to the knee surgery. It feels good to feel good, in total, physically right now.”</p><p>But it hasn’t just been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/01/cubs-matthew-boyd-all-star-ace-starting-rotation-pitching-injuries-craig-counsell-pete-crow-armstrong-alex-bregman-thumbs-down" >The Boyd Show</a>.</p><p>Imanaga has been awesome in July, with a 1.19 ERA in four starts.</p><p>Lefty David Peterson has allowed only five runs combined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/28/cubs-david-peterson-mlb-trade-deadline-mets-jed-hoyer-pitching-staff-rotation-craig-counsell-ground-ball-rate" >in his four good starts</a> since joining the Cubs in a trade.</p><p>Even fill-in righty Colin Rea has had more good moments than bad of late, with a 3.35 ERA in his last seven starts.</p><p>And righty Javier Assad has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/11/cubs-javier-assad-reds-pitching-injuries-rotation-home-runs-craig-counsell-jameson-taillon-phil-maton" >bounced between the bullpen and rotation</a> to the tune of a 2.47 ERA in his last 10 outings.</p><p>It’s a far cry from a month ago, when injuries decimated the starting staff and the Cubs were searching for anyone to make starts. At one point, the team had an entire rotation on the IL, with righties Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown hitting the shelf on the same day in June, when Boyd and Taillon were still making their own recoveries.</p><p>Though they’re not out of the injury woods yet, things are far less hectic on that front.</p><p>With additions likely coming at the deadline, the Cubs could simultaneously find themselves looking at restored depth and enhancements to a group that’s already cooking, a necessity if they’re going to avoid the pitching issues that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-playoffs-brewers-pirates-nl-central-matthew-boyd-starting-rotation" >ended their playoff run earlier than hoped</a> last fall.</p><p>“There was a time when we were like, ‘Who is going to start games for us?’” manager Craig Counsell said Thursday. “This group has stabilized [things]. That’s not a concern.</p><p>“The group has performed. Those questions are gone. But there’s always going to be a quest to get better.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Two more tornadoes confirmed, brings Monday total to 7
entries.summary: <p>The National Weather Service on Thursday confirmed two more tornadoes from Monday’s storms, bringing the total seven as Cook County issued a disaster proclamation due to the "significant damage and disruption" caused by the storms.</p><p>The county's move frees up county resources to local municipalities, including funds, personnel and equipment such as generators, excavators and portable light towers, the county said in a statement Thursday. That's in addition to debris removal and road-clearing; the county said it already has been working with 15 towns and villages that were in the path of the storms.</p><p>Residents impacted have until August 5 to take the <a class="Link" href="https://links-2.govdelivery.com/CL0/https:%2F%2Fsurvey123.arcgis.com%2Fshare%2F56bafe3b44854af192993d73a2201765%3Futm_medium=email%26utm_source=govdelivery/2/0101019fb518f643-6cdbed24-a18d-4209-a646-03b4e159ab69-000000/ugIhOGrOYsLNTBXAxvakfaF_j42_CkMIwNMu-YedaS4=452" target="_blank" >Cook County Resident Damage Survey</a> online to report damages and possibly receive assistance.</p><p>It comes as the weather service said Hazel Crest and Lansing saw EF-1 tornadoes, while Glen Ellyn, Wheaton, Downers Grove, Orland Park and Romeoville — where NWS has its nearest office to the city — saw EF-0 tornadoes.</p><p>Eastern Will County saw straight-line winds of up to 100 mph, and eastern Lake County, Illinois, saw up to 90 mph winds, which could potentially have been tornadoes. However, the weather service said it was “unable to confirm additional tornadoes at this time.”</p><p>“There may have been additional brief tornadoes in southern Cook County and into northwest Indiana along the northern side of an expansive surge of extreme straight-line winds,” the service said in a statement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Our survey data can be viewed here: <a href="https://t.co/jeDwnPBO0Y">https://t.co/jeDwnPBO0Y</a> <a href="https://t.co/4soo3p9D16">https://t.co/4soo3p9D16</a></p>— NWS Chicago (@NWSChicago) <a href="https://x.com/NWSChicago/status/2082925825129611624?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Four of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/28/storms-flooding-tornadoes-damage-worker-missing-power-outage" target="_blank" ><u>tornadoes</u></a> touched down in the south and west suburbs.</p><p>Lansing was hit by one, while another traveled through Country Club Hills, Hazel Crest, Harvey and Homewood with gusts up to 110 mph, according to the weather service. Two other confirmed tornadoes touched down in Glen Ellyn and Orland Park, each with winds reaching 85 mph.</p><p>An EF-0 tornado also touched down just south of Wheaton College with 75 mph winds surrounded by straight-line thunderstorm winds, according to the weather service. Midway Airport recorded winds of 73 mph and O’Hare Airport saw 65 mph winds that night.</p><p>A much stronger <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/28/wisconsin-tornado" target="_blank" ><u>EF-3 tornado touched down</u></a> further north in the Fox Cities region of Wisconsin — about 100 miles north of Milwaukee — at around 1 p.m. and remained on the ground for more than 20 minutes, cutting a roughly 12-mile path of destruction, the weather service reported.</p>

entries.title: Five years after ABC 7 fired him, Mark Giangreco is 'turned loose'
entries.summary: <p>Mark Giangreco has made countless appearances on ESPN 1000’s “Waddle & Silvy” show, in studio and on the phone. But after ABC 7 made him walk the plank in 2021, those in-person segments disappeared with him. Until this year, ESPN 1000 was based in ABC 7’s building downtown on State Street, and Giangreco was — and likely still is — not welcome.</p><p>“Not allowed in the building,” Giangreco, 74, told the Sun-Times. “I could never just sneak into the radio studio because the way it was set up, you had to go through the back of the set of the television studio. So there’d always be a chance that I’d run into certain people, and nobody wanted that kind of confrontation.”</p><p>So it was great to see Giangreco, a legendary Chicago sports anchor, join Tom Waddle and Marc Silverman last month in ESPN 1000’s new studio in the Chicago Board of Trade Building. Even better was that because the White Sox were playing, “Waddle & Silvy” aired on YouTube, where there are no holds barred.</p><p>Giangreco was in his element, talking candidly about, well, everything.</p><p>“There wasn’t even a dump button,” he said. “It was so raw and a lot of vulgarity. It was like I was turned loose after 45 years.”</p><p>On NFL insiders: “You talk about suck-ups.”</p><p>On Ozzie Guillen: “His English is worse. It keeps getting worse.”</p><p>On LeBron James: “Great career. Just get out. We’re tired of you, you flopping, whiny …”</p><p>And on ABC 7 news anchor Cheryl Burton, who took offense to a joke by Giangreco on the air and complained to management, thus putting the plank in place:</p><p>“It’s been more than five years that I was run out by a hyper-sensitive, super-insecure, untouchable diva and enabled by a cowardice news director and general manager — but I’m way over it.”</p><p>ABC 7 management declined to comment.</p><p>Giangreco said that his rant about Burton was a joke, too.</p><p>“These people do not live rent-free in my head. I don’t care anymore,” he told the Sun-Times. “But I love making fun of it because, as I said, I had a year and a half left on my final contract. I was counting the days to retirement. I had had enough. The business was fading. It was just a depressing place to work. And I had had a tremendous career.</p><p>“So when we reached a financial settlement, it was all good. I got to leave early. What stuck in my craw for a while is the person who had the power to get me fired — that’s so bizarre. We used to make fun of each other all the time on and off the air. And then all of a sudden, she was offended by what I consider to be a pretty benign comment, relatively speaking.”</p><p>At the end of his sportscast Jan. 28, 2021, Giangreco referred to Burton as someone who could “play the ditzy, combative interior decorator” as part of a fictional DIY Network show. It ended up being Giangreco’s last sportscast.</p><p>“The statute of limitations I assume pretty much ran out,” Giangreco said. “I don’t think the people who fired me really care at this point anymore.”</p><p>On the YouTube show, Silverman asked Giangreco an interesting question: If he were to go into a broadcasting hall of fame similar to that of baseball, which station’s cap — NBC 5, where he spent 12 formative years, or ABC 7, where he spent 28 — would he have engraved on his plaque? Giangreco said neither. But with time to think about it, he changed his answer.</p><p>“I should’ve said Channel 5 because the way it ended at Channel 7 really tainted my [time],” he said.</p><p>After being fired, Giangreco said he received offers from NBC 5, WGN 9, radio stations and podcasts, but he didn’t have it in him anymore to do the work.</p><p>“After 50 years in sports media, beginning my sophomore year in college — I got my first full-time job in radio — I had enough,” he said. “I had the greatest career during the greatest time. It was the golden age of Chicago sports, and it ran simultaneously with the golden age of local television in Chicago sports.”</p><p>And though technically he didn’t leave on his terms, he actually did.</p><p>“My brother said, ‘Well, of course you were going to go out this way,’ ” Giangreco said. “ ‘Of course you were going to be fired.’</p><p>“I dreaded having a going-away retirement party hosted at the station by people I hated, people I didn’t respect. I’m like, this is going to be so awkward. You know what? Let’s just get fired. Then I don’t have to have that party.”</p><p>He took care of that and said he’s better off for it.</p><p>“I’m so proud of the fact that I don’t miss it,” he said. “Being on television is not my persona. There’s so many people I know who were forced out; their whole life was being on TV and being recognized. I don’t care about that at all. The older I get, the fewer and fewer people recognize me, and that’s fine.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-saturday/2021/5/8/22423666/mark-giangreco-carol-marin-ron-magers-bob-vorwald-cheryl-burton-michael-jordan-mike-ditka-chicago" >Leaving his Mark: Giangreco’s story plays out like no other</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><h3>Remote patrol</h3><ul id="rte-5f8b89e2-8c62-11f1-8863-213082bff57f"><li>WGN 9 sports anchor Jarrett Payton, the son of Bears great Walter Payton, announced that he’s leaving the station after 10 years to spend more time with his family.</li><li>Eddie Olczyk, the former longtime Blackhawks TV analyst, is leaving the Kraken after four seasons and will limit his schedule to TNT broadcasts.</li><li>Adam Amin, A.J.
